I am 56 years old, and I have worked these 4.5 mu in Quzhou County for 35 years. My university education taught me how to read the science, but experience taught me what actually works on this specific piece of land. It is early spring now, and the winter wheat I sowed last October is greening up after the cold months. With six people in the household and some family members earning off-farm income, I do not need to squeeze every last yuan out of the soil. I farm carefully, not desperately.

For the wheat: I already applied phosphorus and potassium as base fertilizer last autumn—about 6 kg P and 4 kg K per mu. Now I will top-dress nitrogen at green-up and again at jointing, bringing the total nitrogen for this wheat crop to about 15 kg per mu. I have a well, so water is reliable. I will irrigate three times: at green-return, at jointing, and at grain filling. Two pesticide applications will suffice—one targeting weeds and another for aphids or powdery mildew if the weather turns humid. There is no tillage to do now; the crop is already established.

After combining the wheat in early June, I will immediately rotary-till the stubble and plant summer maize. I always use hybrid seed—Zhengdan 958—because it is dependable in our North China Plain heat. For the maize, I will apply about 18 kg N, 5 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu, split between basal dressing and an ear-stage top dressing. I will irrigate three times: at the seedling stage, at tasseling, and at grain filling. Two pesticide applications—one herbicide and one insecticide for corn borer. I am not chasing record yields. I aim for about 550 kg per mu from the wheat and 600 kg per mu from the maize. Pushing harder with extra fertilizer only raises costs and damages the soil I will hand to the next generation.
